why.say:
Okay, quick game, and nobody gets to sit this one out. If your palms are a little sweaty, good. It means you care. On my first day mine were so sweaty I couldn't unlock my own phone.

Here's how it works. I describe a job, you shout who owns it: the client, the attorney, or the Case Manager. Ready?

Deciding whether to settle. Calling the body shop for the estimate. Telling a judge what the case is worth. Making sure the client's MRI report actually lands in the file. {name}, you get the tiebreaker on that last one.

So why do I play this on day one? Because most new Case Managers think the job is answering phones and moving paper.

By the end of this block you'll see it's the job that decides whether a good case gets a great settlement or a sad one. It's the client's case, it's the attorney's judgment, and it's your movement.

And there's one line in this role you must never cross. Hang on, I'll show you exactly where it is.
why.ask: {name}, before I tell you: whose file is it really, the client's, Atty. Thorne's, or yours?

theory.say:
So, what is Case Management? Simply put, you're the person who keeps the case moving from the first phone call to the final check.

You track it, you handle it, and you push it forward, one phase at a time.

Every task you touch has to pass three tests. Is it on time? Is it written down properly in the file? Does everyone who needs to know actually know?

You'll hear the phrase case health analysis a lot. Honestly, it just means stepping back and reading the whole file for trouble, instead of looking at one task at a time.

One kind of Case Manager ticks off today's to-do list and goes home. The other notices the client hasn't been to therapy in twelve days and flags it before the adjuster does.

{name}, which of those two do you think the insurance company is hoping we hire?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these three tests do you think new Case Managers fail most often?

frame.say:
Here's the whole process, laid end to end. Before I walk you through it, a little guessing game.

{name}, out of these six stages, which one do you think most cases get stuck in? Hold that answer.

It starts with intake and case opening. You check the facts, run the Conflict Check, which just means making sure the firm doesn't already represent the other side, and open the file in the CMS.

Then planning, where you draft the Case Plan and Atty. Thorne sets strategy. Documentation runs the whole way through.

Communication means keeping the client, the insurance companies and the doctors updated, and logging every contact the same day. Monitoring means every deadline is on the calendar. Then billing and resolution, and you close a complete file.

So, the answer? It's documentation, almost every time. Missing records are the number one reason a demand goes out late, and a late demand is money left on the table.
frame.ask: {name}, looking at John Doe's file today, which stage is he sitting in right now?

rules.say:
Now the rules, and that line I promised you.

You own the movement: deadlines, documents, insurance companies, doctors, and keeping the client updated. Atty. Thorne owns every legal judgment: what the case is worth, whether it's strong, the strategy, and whether to settle.

Every contact, document and deadline goes in the CMS the same day, because if it isn't in the CMS, it didn't happen.

My first boss said that so often that when I told her I'd gotten engaged, she asked if I'd logged it.

Okay, here's the line. You can explain the process and confirm facts. You can never tell a client what their case is worth or whether to take an offer.

A brand-new Case Manager once told a client, just trying to be nice, "You'll get at least fifty grand." The client held onto that number for eight months.

Every offer after that felt like an insult, and the case nearly blew up. One friendly sentence. That's the line.
rules.ask: {name}, the client asks you, “Should I take what they're offering?” What do you say, word for word?

model.say:
This is the picture I want you carrying around all week, and there's a little secret hiding in it. I'll get to that.

Across the slide is the case lifecycle, eight stations left to right: Intake, Claim Set-Up, Treatment, Pre-Demand, Demand, Settlement and Liens, Disbursement, and Litigation.

Liens, by the way, are just bills that get paid out of the settlement before the client gets their share. Litigation is drawn dashed because it's the fork, the road a case only takes if it doesn't settle.

Above the track, the navy band says the Case Manager owns the movement. Below it, the orange band says Atty. Thorne owns every legal judgment.

Now the secret. See that little CMS monitor under the first station? That's the most important thing on the slide.

{name}, why do you think the CMS sits under station one and not station eight?
model.ask: {name}, which station on this track do you think is the easiest place to lose a client's trust?

job.say:
So here's how it really runs on the job. A new case gets assigned to you.

The tempting move is to grab the phone and call the client right away to say hi. The better move is to read the raw file end to end in the CMS first, so every party, date and insurance company is noted before you dial.

Trust me on this. On my first day I was so nervous I called a client and introduced myself as him.

Then, a week in, the client asks you a legal question. You log it in the Communications Log, create a task, and send it to Atty. Thorne that same day, with the facts and no opinion from you.

Deadlines and risks go on the Calendar and under Risk Flags, with a next step.

Why bother? Because the adjuster reads our file history like a report card. A clean, logged file says we're organized and ready to go to court. A messy one says we'll take a lowball.

So here's your mystery for the next block. John Doe's file already has one detail in it that could cost him money if nobody catches it. {name}, your job is to find it before I do.
job.ask: {name}, what's the first thing you'd check on a brand-new file, and why that one?

why.say:
Let's play Five-Minute Detective. A brand-new file just landed on your desk, and you get five questions before the phone rings. What do you ask?

Shout them out, I'm keeping score. {name}, you go first. {name}, give me one nobody's said yet.

Nice. Who got hurt, when, who's insured and for how much, and what could go wrong. That's the list every great Case Manager runs in their head.

And here's the thing. Every lesson, activity and Learning Check this week works one single file, John Doe v. Robert Smith. Know its facts cold and every click in the CMS will make sense.

Now, remember the mystery I left you with? There's one detail on this file that can change how much money John Doe can reach.

I'm not telling you what it is. By the end of this block, you'll find it yourselves.
why.ask: {name}, if you only got one question before the phone rang, which one would you ask, and why that one?

theory.say:
Four ideas, nice and simple.

First, the Case Snapshot. Think of it as the file's ID card: the parties, the date of loss, the statute of limitations, which is just the legal deadline to sue, the client's position and the insurance, all on one card.

Second, the Facts of Loss: how, where and when the crash happened, backed up by the Police Report and witnesses.

Third, the Critical Case Event, the one fact the other side will build their whole defense on. You spot it early so Atty. Thorne can plan around it.

Fourth, the source documents: the intake sheet, the supplement and the Police Report.

Somebody new says, "I'm pretty sure the crash was on a Tuesday." Somebody good says, "Police Report, page one, 02/06/2026."

I once heard a Case Manager argue a date with an adjuster for ten minutes, from memory. She lost. You quote the document, never your memory.

And never a sticky note. I once found a client's date of loss on a sticky note glued to the bottom of somebody's coffee mug.
theory.ask: {name}, why do you think the defense cares so much about the Critical Case Event?

frame.say:
Time to run the five questions on John Doe, and this time the answers come from the documents, not from me.

{name}, you're Who. {name}, you're When. Everybody else, you're the fact-checkers.

Who? John Doe is our client, and Robert Smith is the defendant, meaning the person we're making the claim against. Who else was in the car, and where John Doe was sitting, is in the Police Report. Hmm, funny how I keep saying that, isn't it?

What? A collision, and the Run Report, that's the ambulance crew's report, says what they found.

When? 02/06/2026, about 7:10 in the morning, and the legal deadline counts from that exact date. Where? The all-way stop at Maple Hollow Rd and Birch Ave.

And how? Police Report again, including whether anyone got a ticket.

Five questions, five documents. Get one wrong here and it rides all the way into the demand letter.
frame.ask: {name}, which of these five answers will you check first in the Police Report, and why?

rules.say:
Okay, here's what I'll tell you, and what I won't.

The crash happened on 02/06/2026, around 7:10 a.m., at the all-way stop at Maple Hollow Rd and Birch Ave. Our client is John Doe, 34, a warehouse shift lead at Northgate Distribution.

Atty. Elijah Thorne is Lead Counsel, and you're the Case Manager.

Now the money. The Recovery Stack, which just means every insurance policy that could pay, stacked in the order they pay, is $40,000 across three layers: BI, Host UM, Relative UM.

Say it with me. Again. Love it.

Now the teaser. Which of those layers can he actually reach? That depends on where he was sitting, and I'm not telling you. It's in the Police Report.

Same with the gap between the ambulance date and his first doctor visit. Find it yourself.

The bare-minimum Case Manager waits for someone to hand them the answer. The really good one goes and reads.
rules.ask: {name}, no notes: what are the three layers of the stack, in order?

model.say:
This is John Doe's file at a glance, laid out like a folder.

Top left, the name of the case, John Doe v. Robert Smith, with matter number LSH-2026-MVA-770412 underneath. On the left, the all-way stop at Maple Hollow Rd and Birch Ave.

On the right, three stacked bars for the $40,000: BI $10,000, Host UM $20,000, Relative UM $10,000.

Along the bottom there's an orange strip from the date of loss to his first treatment. How long it is? That's yours to work out.

Now look at what's missing. The card doesn't say where he sat, or who got the ticket. {name}, why do you think I left those off?

Because those two blanks are worth real money. If he was in his own car, he may reach far less. If he was a passenger, a whole extra layer can open up.

One blank field, thousands of dollars.
model.ask: {name}, which document will you open first to fill in the blanks on this card?

job.say:
Here's how it plays out for real.

Your first job is to read the Case File profile and the intake documents until you can say the date of loss, the stack and the critical fact from memory.

Then the matter opens in the CMS, and now memory isn't good enough. Every fact you enter has to point back to a document.

And when a fact changes later, and trust me, it will, you update Case Notes and tell the team the same day. Not the sticky note on your monitor. Monitors get bumped, and sticky notes lose their sticky right when you need them.

Quick war story. I had a client who told intake he was driving. Turned out he was in the back seat and his cousin was driving.

Nobody checked the Police Report for three weeks. Three weeks of letters to the wrong insurance company.

So why does it matter? Because the adjuster's first offer is built on what's in our file. Wrong facts, wrong stack, smaller check.
job.ask: {name}, if a fact on the file changes on Thursday, who needs to know, and by when?

dodont.say:
Game time: 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides a Do or a Don't about knowing your case.

Three clues come up one at a time. Shout it the moment you know it, Do or Don't, and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it.

{name}, you're keeping score. {name}, you're on the first buzz.

While we play, one thought. A gap in treatment isn't anybody's failing. People work, they wait, they hope the pain goes away.

A careless Case Manager judges it. A great one documents it, with dates, so Atty. Thorne can explain it before the adjuster uses it against us.

And here's your mystery for the rest of today. The Police Report tells you where John Doe was sitting. Who finds it first, and what does it unlock?
dodont.ask: {name}, before you open the report, make your guess: driver or passenger, and what's your evidence?

why.say:
Let's play Guess the Price. A brand-new Case Manager makes one mistake in the first hour of opening a file. One field, typed wrong.

How much money do you think that mistake can cost the client? Shout a number. {name}? Okay, {name}, higher or lower?

I'll reveal it at the end of this block, and honestly, you'll be surprised. Here's your hint: the field is the client's position in the vehicle, where he was sitting.

Intake is where you take control of the file. It's not just typing in data. A file opened wrong stays wrong, because every deadline, every demand letter and every lien check reads from the fields you set in that first hour.

A lien, by the way, is just a bill that gets paid out of the settlement before the client sees a dime.

So a mixed-up party isn't a typo. It can be a whole insurance policy the client never gets to.
why.ask: {name}, what do you think is the most expensive mistake you could make in the first hour of a new file?

map.say:
Here's where this lesson is going, so nothing surprises you later. Opening a file runs in six steps.

Seven, if you count remembering your CMS password. And no, it's still not Password1. {name}, you're on step one.

First, the Conflict Check, which means checking every party's full legal name to make sure the firm isn't already working for the other side. You do it before the file even exists.

Second, you verify the facts, starting with the date of loss against the Police Report. Third, you put the statute of limitations, the legal deadline to sue, on the calendar on day one.

Fourth, you match every person to their role and record where the client was sitting. Fifth, you record the insurance from the Declaration Page, with where you found it. Sixth, you name and file every document.

A rushed file skips step one and gets to step six whenever. A strong file does all six, in order, on day one.
map.ask: {name}, which of these six steps do you think gets skipped most often on a busy day?

theory.say:
Vocabulary time, and I promise to keep it simple.

The Recovery Stack is every insurance policy that can pay the claim, stacked in the order it pays. You find every layer at intake, not later.

Bodily Injury Liability, or BI, is the at-fault driver's insurance for injuries he causes other people. It pays first. That's called a third-party claim, because we're claiming against someone else's policy.

UM and UIM is coverage for when the at-fault driver has no insurance or not enough. It's first-party, meaning it comes from the car or the household the client is connected to.

And then exclusions and rejections. A signed paper turning down UM, or a rule that excludes a car, can close a layer completely. When that happens, you write down the exact document that did it.

{name}, quick check: if Robert Smith's policy is too small, where do we look next?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these terms is new to you, and which one do you think trips people up?

theory2.say:
A few more terms, and these are the ones people mix up constantly.

MedPay and PIP are medical coverage from the client's side that pays no matter who caused the crash. They pay bills early, while the claim's still open.

Property Damage liability fixes what the at-fault driver damaged, and collision is the owner's own coverage for their car. Neither one joins the injury stack.

Next, limits. A split limit, say twenty-five, fifty, caps each injured person at the first number and the whole accident at the second. So you read both.

I once watched a Case Manager tell the whole team we had fifty thousand available. We had twenty-five. That was an awkward meeting.

And the Declaration Page, or Dec Page, is the insurance company's own statement of who's insured, which cars, what coverage and what limits. That's your proof, not someone's summary.
theory2.ask: {name}, on a split limit, which of the two numbers caps one injured person's claim?

frame.say:
This is the intake workflow, five steps. {name}, you're my narrator. Tell me if I skip one.

The raw file comes in from On the Records, and you read it end to end before anything else. Then you check the details, the date of loss, the parties and the signatures, against the Police Report, not the intake note.

Next, the Conflict Check, on every party's full legal name, with the date and result written down.

Then a decision. Complete intake moves forward to acceptance. Incomplete intake goes back. If you're not sure the case qualifies, it goes to Atty. Thorne.

Only then is the file created in the CMS, with six roles mapped, the deadline on the calendar, and documents named.

I get it, the boss wants the file today, so it's tempting to jump straight to creating it. Take the ten extra minutes instead and open it right once.
frame.ask: {name}, on John Doe's file right now, which of these five steps has actually been done?

rules.say:
You're the gatekeeper of case quality, so incomplete intake goes back, not forward.

Run the Conflict Check before the file exists, on the full legal name of every party: Robert Smith, the host driver, the resident relative. Record its date and result.

Confirm the date of loss against the Police Report, because every deadline counts from it, and put the statute of limitations on the calendar on day one: 02/06/2028.

Compare the story with the Police Report and the client's statement, check every signature, and never quietly fix a mismatch.

Map all six roles. An "unknown" party is just a layer you haven't found yet. Record where the client was sitting, and get the emergency contact.

Read the insurance off the Declaration Page and note every source. Name documents the firm's way. And you never tell the client what the case is worth.

{name}, which of these would hurt most if you skipped it?
rules.ask: {name}, why does the Conflict Check have to happen before the file is created, not just soon after?

model.say:
Look at the contrast here. On the left, a messy grey stack called raw intake. In the middle, three gates: verify, map, structure.

On the right, a clean CMS matter card with six role rows, each with a green tick. Underneath, the case's four anchors.

Okay, now the reveal I promised you on the first slide. A client driving his own car may only reach his own policy. A passenger in someone else's car can reach that car's coverage too, and sometimes a relative's.

Same crash, same injuries, and the money available can be four times larger, all decided by one field. That's the price of the mistake.

{name}, was your guess high enough?

So which is John Doe, driver or passenger? Nope, not telling. Read the Police Report and record it yourself.
model.ask: {name}, what would have happened to John Doe's recovery if someone had left his position as “driver”?

job.say:
Let's follow a real day. The raw file arrives from On the Records. You log into the CMS on the first try, which on a Monday is already a win.

Before the file even exists, you run and record the Conflict Check in CMS New Case. Then you check the date of loss, the parties and the signatures against the documents.

Once the matter's created, you put the deadline, 02/06/2028, on the Calendar. You log the retainer, that's the signed agreement that hires us, and the HIPAA authorization, the client's signed permission for us to get his medical records, in Documents.

As people are identified, you map all six roles in Parties, and nobody stays "unknown".

As documents arrive, you name each one the firm's way and file it, so anyone can find it by name.

War story. I once inherited a file where every document was named "scan.pdf". Forty-one of them. It took me a full afternoon to find the Police Report.
job.ask: {name}, why do you think naming a document correctly matters to the settlement, not just to us?

dodont.say:
Round time: 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides one of this lesson's Dos or Don'ts about intake.

Clues come up one by one. Call Do or Don't and name the rule as fast as you can. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it.

{name} and {name}, you two are going head to head on round one.

While you play, remember that files from On the Records arrive unverified. A sloppy Case Manager treats the intake note as gospel and carries its mistakes straight into the demand. A sharp one treats it as a rumor until a document proves it.

And the UPL line comes back every single day. You confirm facts and explain the process. You never say what the case is worth.

Your mystery for the next activity: a colleague already typed John Doe's draft record, and it has mistakes in it. How many, and which one costs the most?
dodont.ask: {name}, make a prediction: how many mistakes do you think are hiding in that draft record?

why.say:
Quick game to start. I say a sentence, and you give me a thumbs up if it belongs in a Case Plan, thumbs down if it doesn't. Ready?

The client has a 14-day gap in treatment. The client is a really nice guy. The other driver ran a red light, according to the Police Report. This case is worth a fortune.

{name}, I saw that face on the last one, so you're my tiebreaker.

So why this game? The Case Plan is the file's instruction manual. It's what Atty. Thorne reads to set strategy, and it's what every later day of this course works from.

If the plan hides a risk, the whole strategy gets built on a fake picture, and nobody finds out until it's expensive.

In a minute I'll show you the plan's layout. One part of it is drawn bigger than everything else, and in red. {name}, keep your eyes peeled for it, because that's the whole lesson in one picture.
why.ask: {name}, what happens if Atty. Thorne builds a demand strategy without knowing about the 14-day gap?

theory.say:
Early evaluation really comes down to three simple questions. Is there money? Who's responsible? And how is this case likely to move?

Coverage determination is the first one. It means checking which insurance policies apply, what they pay, how high they go, and what they exclude. Basically, is there money to pay the claim?

Liability assessment is the second: who caused the crash and how much, whether it's clear, shared or disputed, and what evidence backs it.

Case projection is the third. It's an early read on risk and where the case is heading, but the value of the case stays with the attorney, always.

One more idea. Once a case is in a legal setting, Case Management stops being "I'll do my best" and becomes strict compliance. Every deadline in the plan goes on the calendar, no exceptions.

{name}, quick guess before I tell you: which of these three questions do you think gets answered wrong most often on brand-new files?
theory.ask: {name}, why can't a projection come before we understand coverage and liability?

frame.say:
These three pillars only work together, and there's a reason they're in this order. I'll make you guess it at the end.

Coverage asks, is there money to pay the claim? That means valid policies, what type of coverage, the limits, the exclusions and any gaps.

Liability asks, who's responsible, and how much? Who caused it, is it clear, shared or disputed, what's the evidence, and is there comparative negligence, which just means the client might be blamed for part of the crash too.

Projection asks, how is this case likely to move? It pulls from everything: coverage, liability, how bad the injury is, what treatment we expect, and how good our paperwork is.

So, {name}, why is projection last? Because it leans on the other two.

A projection without coverage and liability is like guessing the score of a game before you know who's playing.
frame.ask: {name}, on John Doe's file today, which of these three questions can you actually answer with a document?

rules.say:
Now the rules, and I'll show you what so-so looks like next to what excellent looks like.

Acceptance comes first. You decide: Accepted, Escalated for review, or Declined, with a reason someone else can follow.

A so-so Case Manager leaves the file in limbo for a week, still "gathering info." An excellent one makes the call, and escalates anything unclear with a short note saying exactly what.

Write coverage, liability and projection together, and keep the projection preliminary until coverage is confirmed. Liability isn't final until the Police Report, the driver statements and any video back it up, so never tell a client it's a sure thing.

Same goes for the client who says "I feel fine now" two weeks before his MRI. Lovely news, not a medical finding, so it doesn't change the plan.

Hold a place for the Regulatory Triple-Check, three checks on privacy, Medicare and who pays first, which we clear in the Treatment Phase. File the Three-Pillar plan inside the state's window, often 30 to 60 days, and calendar it.

Every goal gets a measure, an owner and a date. And the big one: flag bad facts loudly. The plan suggests next steps; value and settlement belong to Atty. Thorne. {name}, here's your test.
rules.ask: {name}, can you write “request the MRI” in the plan? What about “worth policy limits”?

model.say:
Here it is, the reveal. The plan has five bands stacked top to bottom, each with an orange number.

One is the Case Snapshot and the acceptance decision. Two is coverage, liability and projection. Three is the Regulatory Triple-Check, held open until the Treatment Phase. Four is the Three-Pillar Plan, split into Clinical, Functional and Financial columns.

And five, the one I promised you, is Risks and Flags. It's red, it's visibly taller than the rest, and it holds one highlighted chip: 14-Day Treatment Gap.

That's on purpose. On a Case Plan, the bad news gets more room than the good news.

To the right, a routing line runs to a card that reads Atty. Elijah Thorne, review, with a calendar chip under it: file within 30 to 60 days.

I once saw a plan where the risks section just said "none." Three weeks later the adjuster found the gap the Case Manager already knew about. That conversation was not fun.

{name}, tell the room why that red band is the biggest one.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think the risks band is drawn taller than the band holding the plan itself?

job.say:
Let me take you through a real day on the desk. The verification call is done, so you record the acceptance decision in Case Notes: Accepted, Escalated or Declined, with a reason a co-worker could follow without calling you.

If your note needs a translator, you've written it like a doctor's prescription.

Once coverage is confirmed in writing, you open the Action Plan Editor, which is just the screen in the CMS where the plan gets written, and you draft all five bands. The risks band is never empty.

Then you put the filing window on the CMS Calendar and send the plan to Atty. Thorne from the editor, before anything goes out that commits the firm to a position.

Why does this matter so much? Because that 14-day gap, flagged on day one, is something Atty. Thorne can explain in the demand.

Found by the adjuster on day ninety, it's a reason to cut the offer. Same fact, very different settlement. {name}, you're up first on this one.
job.ask: {name}, what's the very first thing you'd write in the risks band for John Doe, and why that?

dodont.say:
Let's close with a game called 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides one Do or Don't about acceptance and the Case Plan.

I'll show three clues, one at a time. Call Do or Don't and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it. {name}, you're captain of the left side of the room.

Keep one line in mind while you play. "Request the MRI" is operational, so it's yours. "This case is worth policy limits," meaning the most the insurance will ever pay, is never yours to write.

And I know flagging a risk can feel like admitting the case is weak. It isn't. Flagging early is exactly what makes a case defensible later.

Okay, your mystery before we move on. That 14-Day Treatment Gap chip is sitting in red, and John Doe still hasn't seen a doctor since the crash. Nobody has written down what's stopping him.

{name}, by the end of the next block, I want your best theory, backed by something already on the file.
dodont.ask: {name}, what's one fact on John Doe's file that might explain why he hasn't seen a doctor?

why.say:
Let's start with a game called Good Intentions, Bad Outcome. I name something a brand-new client does in week one. Thumbs up if it helps the claim, thumbs down if it hurts it. Ready?

Posting a gym selfie to show they're tough. Chatting with the other driver's insurance to be polite. Skipping physical therapy because they feel a bit better.

Whoa, {name}, you were fast on that last one.

Here's what gets me. Every single one of those came from a nice person trying to do the right thing.

So here's the teaser. Most of the damage to an injury claim happens in the first two weeks, before anyone has told the client what not to do.

By the end of this block you'll know the three mistakes clients make most, and I'll show you which one has already started on John Doe's file.

You give the instructions. What any of it means for the claim is Atty. Thorne's to explain.
why.ask: {name}, what's one thing a new client might do in week one, meaning well, that could hurt the claim?

theory.say:
Here's the road for this lesson, four stops.

First, the standing instructions: no recorded call with the other side's insurance, no posts, and nothing signed until we've looked at it. Second, treatment: keep every appointment, and tell us about any problem getting there before a visit is missed.

Third, receipts, because only what's written down can be claimed. Fourth, the car, which is the one exception.

Now the big idea underneath. Anything a client says, posts, signs or skips can become evidence.

A Recorded Statement, by the way, is just the insurance company taping the client's version of the crash, and they can use every word later. And the Letter of Representation is the letter that tells the other side, from now on, you talk to us, not our client.

{name}, quick guess before I answer: what's the difference between a medical danger and a legal danger?

Okay. A medical danger threatens his health, like a fever after surgery, so the doctor's office hears about it today. A legal danger threatens the claim, like three weeks with no therapy, so Atty. Thorne hears about it today. Same urgency, different phone call.
theory.ask: {name}, can you give me an example of a legal danger that isn't a medical one?

rules.say:
These are the firm's standing instructions, and I want you to hear the difference between doing them on autopilot and doing them well.

The client gives no Recorded Statement to the other driver's insurance; all their contact comes through us. They start treatment, keep every appointment, and tell you about any barrier, like rides, money or work, before a visit is missed.

They post nothing about the crash, the injuries or their activities, and sign nothing until we've reviewed it. They keep every receipt, even mileage.

Autopilot is emailing a PDF and calling it done. Doing it well means going through each rule on the phone, having the client say it back to you, and logging that they understood.

And yes, clients will argue that a gym selfie proves they're recovering. To an adjuster, it proves they can deadlift, and the offer drops to match.

Is it worth the extra effort? Absolutely. One recorded call can hand the adjuster a quote like "I'm fine, really," and that one sentence can shave thousands off the offer at the end.
rules.ask: {name}, if John Doe asks why he shouldn't give a Recorded Statement, what can you say without giving legal advice?

model.say:
Here's the board. Green Do column on the left, red Don't column on the right, and each Don't lines up with the Do that replaces it.

why.say:
Quick game. I'll say a sentence clients say to us every single week, and you tell me true or false. Ready? “I've got full coverage, so I'm fine.”

{name}, true or false? Take a second.

The answer: there's no such thing. People say full coverage the way they say “I'm almost ready” when they haven't found their shoes. Every policy pays a different thing.

So here are two questions, and I want them as two columns in your head. Who pays the bills now? And who pays the claim later? People mix them up all the time, and that's exactly where the money leaks out.

There's a rule called the Payer-First Principle, which just means each bill goes to the payer that has to pay it first.

Get the order right and a bill gets paid once, cheaply. Get it wrong and that same bill comes back later as a lien, a bill paid out of John Doe's settlement.

And I'll show you one $2,395 bill on this file where the order made all the difference.
why.ask: {name}, who pays John Doe's bills now, and who pays his claim later? Are they the same?

theory.say:
Every policy answers two questions: whose is it, and what does it pay?

Third-party coverage belongs to the at-fault driver, and here that's Robert Smith. First-party coverage answers to the client's side. Who you're claiming against changes how you talk to them, because one is on our side and one very much isn't.

Next, the Recovery Stack. That's only the coverage that pays the claim itself: BI, which is bodily injury coverage on the at-fault driver, then the UM and UIM layers, the coverage that steps in when the at-fault driver has too little or no insurance. Medical Bills and the car sit outside the stack.

Then there's no-fault medical coverage, MedPay and PIP. It pays accident Medical Bills no matter who caused the crash, and fast.

And here's the twist that surprises everyone: UM follows the person, not the car. {name}, that's going to matter in a minute, because John Doe has no car policy of his own.
theory.ask: {name}, John Doe reaches two UM policies, and neither is his own. Which status gets him to each one?

theory2.say:
Four more ideas, and I'll keep them simple.

First, set-off and non-duplication. Some policies subtract what PIP or MedPay already paid from what they owe, so you verify that in writing.

Second, subrogation. That's a fancy word for a payer's right to get its money back out of the settlement. A payer with subrogation wants repaying. A payer without it doesn't, and what it paid stays paid.

Third, contract rate and write-off. When a doctor is in-network, they accept the Health Plan's price and write off the rest, so the client isn't billed the difference and the lien is smaller.

Fourth, Medicare Secondary Payer. Medicare pays only after the no-fault and liability coverage, it gets repaid by law, and the case gets reported to the BCRC, the federal office that tracks this.

The joke I tell new hires: the fine print on a policy is printed in a font designed by the same people who make prescription bottle labels. {name}, that's exactly why we read it anyway.
theory2.ask: {name}, why is a payer with no right to be paid back the best one to bill first?

frame.say:
Here's the table, row by row. Before I go through it, {name}, guess which row pays John Doe's bills fastest. Hold that.

BI liability is the at-fault driver's, third-party, and it pays the claim for the injuries he caused. UM and UIM sit on the client's side, through the vehicle or the household, and pay when BI is too small, with consent rules that protect their right to be repaid.

PIP comes from the policy on the vehicle the client was riding in, and pays Medical Bills without anyone proving fault, though not lost wages; its repayment terms you verify in writing. Where a state requires PIP with wages, it can pay part of wages and services too.

Health insurance is the client's own plan, at the contract rate, with a right to be repaid. Medicare and Medicaid come last, repaid by law, with a BCRC report.

And the answer to my question? PIP. Fast, and with nothing to repay on this file.

Reading eight policies side by side is like reading eight phone contracts. Every single one has an asterisk, and the asterisk is where the money is.
frame.ask: {name}, which row on this table pays John Doe's bills fastest, with the least to repay?

rules.say:
Here's how you sort every coverage, and you sort it twice.

First by whose. Keystone BI and PD are Robert Smith's, third-party. Host UM, Relative UM and PIP answer to John Doe's side. Bluewater's collision is Margaret's. Peach State is his own Health Plan.

Then by what it pays. BI and UM pay the claim, and only they make the $40,000 stack. PIP pays bills, and a share of lost wages, regardless of fault. This file has Harbor Point PIP, $5,000, on the Escape John rode in, and you verify it.

John reaches Host UM as an occupant of Kevin Alvarez's Escape, and Relative UM as Margaret Doe's resident relative, meaning he lives in her household. Margaret's Bluewater UM was rejected on 03/14/2024.

The bill order: PIP first, because Harbor Point confirmed on 03/02/2026 it has no right to be repaid; then the Health Plan; a Letter of Protection last.

Sending every bill to whoever answers the phone is how liens get born. Route each bill in order and keep a ledger for every payer. And when two policies fight over who pays, that's Atty. Thorne's call.
rules.ask: {name}, before I tell you: where does PIP sit, and why does it go ahead of Peach State?

Green is health: Peach State Health Plan. And a grey card, crossed out: Bluewater UM, rejected 03/14/2024.

Every card is tagged the claim, the bills or the car, and only the three claim cards are bracketed as the $40,000 Recovery Stack.

Below, a staircase steps down the bill order: MedPay or PIP, then the Health Plan, then the Letter of Protection. The callout says it plainly: out of order means a lien that didn't have to exist.

Now, that card that fools everybody. Keystone PD at $25,000 is the biggest number on the slide, and it isn't in the stack at all. {name}, that's your trap to dodge.

job.say:
Here's how it runs across a normal week. As each claim opens, you list every coverage, its carrier and what it pays in the CMS Insurance tab, and tag it third-party, first-party or health.

A doctor's office asks who to bill, and you route it in order using the PIP Log: PIP, then Peach State, then a Letter of Protection.

map.say:
Before the detail, here's the road, five stops.

One, draft one LOR per insurance company on the firm's template, and each one names that company's own insured, meaning their own customer.

Two, each letter asks for the limits and the Declaration Page, which is the policy's one-page summary, and asks them to preserve photos, statements, video and the car's data. Three, protect the client: the letter to the other driver's insurance gets his name and nothing more.

Four, send each one the way that company prefers, signed by Atty. Thorne and logged by you. Five, if nobody acknowledges it by the third business day, you follow up.

Five steps, three carriers, one day.

And my favorite real-life moment on step four: the letter is ready, the clock is ticking, and the one person who has to sign it is always, always at lunch. {name}, that's why you plan the signature before the deadline, not at it.

theory.say:
Claim set-up is really coverage determination. In other words, finding out which policies apply, how much they pay, and what they won't cover.

The LOR is how the firm gets onto each one. It's formal notice that we represent the client, and it moves all contact onto us.

Coverage determination comes down to four questions. Is the coverage valid? What type applies? What are the limits? Are there exclusions, meaning things the policy refuses to cover? Every request in an LOR chases one of those answers.

Then there's liability assessment, which asks who's legally responsible and by how much. Atty. Thorne weighs that; you secure the proof.

And remember first-party versus third-party. The third-party insurer, Robert Smith's, is on the other side. The first-party policies cover our client. So each letter reads differently.

One crash, three insurance companies, and every one of them is convinced one of the others should be paying. {name}, hang on to that picture.
theory.ask: {name}, why would a letter to Robert Smith's carrier read differently from one to Harbor Point?

theory2.say:
Four more ideas.

First, information protection. The other side's insurance company learns only what it must, because anything you hand them can be used against the client.

Second, notice versus demand. A notice says, heads up, there's a claim coming, and it protects our right to make one. A demand asks for money. UM notice goes out early; the UM demand waits until BI has offered its full limit in writing.

Third, the preservation request asks the insurer to keep photos, statements, video, the vehicle and its event data, the car's little black box. That's the liability proof that can vanish if nobody asks.

Fourth, the acknowledgement. That's the insurer's written receipt of your LOR, and sometimes it states the coverage and the limit. It's the first written answer you'll log.

You can send the letter and forget it. Or you can send it, calendar the acknowledgement, and chase it. {name}, be honest, which one sounds like you on a Friday afternoon?
theory2.ask: {name}, what's the difference between putting a UM carrier on notice and making a demand on it?

frame.say:
Coverage and liability run side by side, four questions each. Here's a challenge: {name}, after this slide, tell me which of these eight you can already answer from John Doe's file.

On the coverage side: is there valid insurance? What type applies? What are the policy limits? Are there exclusions or gaps?

On the liability side: who caused the crash? Is fault clear, shared or disputed? What evidence supports it? And are there comparative negligence factors, which just means could the client be blamed for part of it?

Every request in your LORs is chasing one of these eight answers. Keep both columns in your head as you draft, because a letter that only asks about money leaves the liability proof unprotected. And if the camera footage gets erased, no amount of money questions brings it back.

I once had a client point proudly to a fat folder of policy paperwork and say, “See, I'm covered for everything.” It was his renter's insurance. For an apartment he moved out of in 2019.
frame.ask: {name}, which of these eight questions can you answer today on John Doe's file, and from what document?

Let's play Guess the Status. I'm putting five words on the board, in order: reported, noticed, acknowledged, disclosed, confirmed in writing.

I give you a date and an insurance company, and you tell me where it really stood. Ready? Keystone's BI limit on 03/11/2026. {name}, your guess? {name}, do you agree?

The reveal: not confirmed. Not even close. Nobody on this file had seen Keystone's Declaration Page until 03/20/2026.

Both UM carriers had confirmed in writing by 03/09/2026, but the company that pays first was the slowest to prove it.

That's the lesson in one sentence. A coverage fact nobody has verified is just a guess the whole file is built on.

And a phone call where an adjuster says “I think it's ten” is not proof. It's a rumor with a claim number.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to look at any coverage line and tell me in five seconds whether it's proof or a guess.

theory.say:
Coverage verification, simply put, is turning “someone told me” into “here's the document,” with every limit, form and exclusion traced to the paper that proves it.

The Coverage Matrix is one row per insurance company, and it's the file's single coverage record. Status, source and date on every row show what's proven.

The statuses run reported, noticed, acknowledged, disclosed, confirmed in writing, and only the last one is proof. Every earlier one is a lead.

The Declaration Page, the Dec Page, is the policy's own summary of who and what it covers, and for how much. It's the one page in insurance written to be read, and even then the important line is somewhere near the bottom, in a font that requires reading glasses.

Then limit types. Per person caps one injured person. Per accident caps everyone in the crash put together. A combined single limit is one number for all of it.

{name}, those three phrases sound alike and pay very differently.
theory.ask: {name}, Keystone's BI is $10,000 per person. Whose claim does that figure cap?

theory2.say:
A bit deeper now, and there's a $10,000 trap hiding in here.

UM forms come in two kinds. Add-on, also called excess, UM pays on top of what BI paid. Reduced UM subtracts what BI paid from its own limit. Same limit on paper, very different money.

Only the liability and UM layers stack. PIP, PD and collision are separate benefits you track on their own.

Exclusions and gaps matter as much as limits. A verified zero, like a signed rejection form, is a fact. An assumed zero is a guess.

And when an insurer stalls, treat it like any bottleneck: find the root cause, act now, then prevent the next one. “They didn't call back” is a shrug. “They need the signed authorization; I sent it today and set a follow-up for Thursday” is a plan.

{name}, here's the trap. If Harbor Point's UM were the reduced kind, what happens to our total?
theory2.ask: {name}, if Harbor Point's UM had been the reduced form, what would the stack total have been?

frame.say:
Here's every possible coverage source, and what proves it. Before I start, {name}, guess which one on John Doe's file is still missing its proof.

BI liability: per person, per accident or combined, proven by a Dec Page or a Coverage Letter. It's the first layer, and you confirm there's no step-down, a clause that shrinks the limit in certain situations.

Host UM: add-on or reduced, proven by the insurer's written form confirmation, and it opens after BI offers its limit.

Relative UM: the same question plus an other-insurance clause, the part of a policy that says who pays first when two policies cover the same crash. It's proven by a certified policy and Coverage Letter, and which one pays first is Atty. Thorne's call.

MedPay or PIP pays Medical Bills to its limit regardless of fault, proven by its written terms, tracked separately. PD and collision cover the car only, outside the stack. And the client's own UM is zero only if it was rejected in writing, proven by the signed form.

I once had a client insist he had UM because his agent “basically said so at a barbecue.” Barbecues are not Declaration Pages.
frame.ask: {name}, which of these six sources on John Doe's file still lacks the document that proves it?

rules.say:
The rules. The Coverage Matrix is the single record: carrier, insured, claim number, adjuster, limit and type, status, source, date and next follow-up.

A limit is preliminary until a Dec Page or Coverage Letter confirms it. A phone figure or a number in the Police Report is a lead, and you never quote it to John Doe.

Read the Dec Page line by line, including a policy period that covers 02/06/2026. Keystone's shows BI $10,000 per person. Ask each UM insurer for its form in writing; Harbor Point confirmed add-on on 03/02/2026.

Stack only three layers: $10,000 plus $20,000 plus $10,000, which is $40,000. Verify the gaps too: the Bluewater rejection from 03/14/2024 goes in the file.

Firm timing: 24 to 48 hours on an unopened claim, the third business day on an LOR, and a dated next follow-up within two business days. Legal deadlines, policy duties and bad-faith questions go to Atty. Thorne to confirm.

Why so strict? Because the demand is built on these numbers. One wrong limit and the demand asks for money that doesn't exist. {name}, that is a very awkward phone call.

why.say:
Quick show of hands. Who here has ever had a health insurance company pay a bill, and then months later send a letter saying, actually, we'd like some of that back?

Keep them up if it made you mad. Yeah. {name}, I see you. Hold onto that feeling, because that's this whole lesson.

I've drawn two lanes on the board. Lane one: who pays John Doe's Medical Bills while the claim is open? Lane two: who pays the claim itself at the end?

Most of the confusion on this topic is just those two questions being treated as one. The Health Plan answers the first question, and then it asks to be paid back out of the second.

So here's my teaser. If a Health Plan's claim for repayment gets discovered after the demand goes out, guess whose pocket the money comes out of?

Not ours. Not the insurer's. I'll tell you in a minute, and it's going to sting.
why.ask: {name}, who pays John Doe's Medical Bills while his claim is open, and who pays the claim itself?

theory.say:
Here's the road first, then the words.

Three checks come before any planning of medical care: a HIPAA authorization written for this claim, the Medicare and Medicaid check, and the Payer Order, which is just the order bills get sent in: PIP first, then health insurance, then a Letter of Protection or liens.

Then the Health Plan's right to be repaid gets flagged the first time we hear about it, and logged in the CMS lien register that same day.

Now the words. Subrogation is a payer's right to get back what it paid for accident care. Primary payer determination decides who gets billed first, so nothing gets paid twice.

A Letter of Protection promises a doctor payment from the settlement, and it comes last. And the client's net is what John Doe actually keeps once fees, costs and liens are paid.

So, the answer to my teaser? A lien flagged late comes straight out of his net. {name}, that's his money, not ours.
theory.ask: {name}, why do you think a Letter of Protection sits last in the Payer Order?

frame.say:
The Regulatory Triple-Check is three checks, and you clear all three before planning any medical care. Think of it as three locks on the front door.

One, HIPAA, the federal privacy law for medical records. You get an authorization written for this claim, naming the date of the crash, because a standard release form may not be good enough for an injury case.

Two, Medicare and Medicaid. If the client is 65 or older, or gets SSDI, which is Social Security disability, you report the case to the BCRC, the federal office that tracks who repays Medicare.

That avoids federal penalties and settlements that get frozen under a law called MMSEA. It's a 2007 federal rule: if Medicare paid any of the bills, it gets paid back, so we report the case.

Three, subrogation management. Set the Payer Order, PIP or MedPay first, then private health insurance, then LOPs and provider liens. Every bill reaches the right payer and every repayment right shows up early.

{name}, here's a puzzle. John Doe is 34. Does that mean we skip check number two?
frame.ask: {name}, John Doe is 34. So which part of the BCRC check still has to be verified for him?

rules.say:
The rules. Clear the triple-check before medical planning, so the claim's properly set up and you're allowed to act.

HIPAA first: an Authorization to Release Medical Information written for this claim, naming the crash date and allowing contact with legal and insurance parties.

Then Medicare and Medicaid. If the client's 65 or older or on SSDI, you report to the Benefits Coordination and Recovery Center under MMSEA, 2007. John Doe is 34, so you verify his SSDI status and write down the answer.

Then the Payer Order, and verify whether MedPay or PIP applies; never assume. And the Payer Order is not the Recovery Stack. One pays bills, the other pays the claim.

When a Health Plan pays accident bills, flag its repayment right the first time you hear about it, and record the carrier, member ID and group number in the lien register that day.

“I'll deal with liens at the end” sounds reasonable and costs the client money. A dated lien record from day one lets Atty. Thorne negotiate it down from strength.

Never promise a provider or a plan any amount. {name}, that's how good intentions become expensive.
rules.ask: {name}, why flag the Health Plan's repayment right the first time you hear about it, instead of waiting for the demand?

model.say:

The upper lane, in navy, is labelled pays the bills now, the Payer Order: PIP or MedPay, then Peach State Health Plan, then LOPs and provider liens.

The lower lane, in orange, is pays the claim later, the Recovery Stack: BI, then Host UM, then Relative UM, ending at a settlement circle.

Now find that heavy orange arrow curving down from the Health Plan into the settlement. That's the claim for repayment, and that's the lesson. Money goes out to doctors early and comes back out of the settlement at the end.

The clues come one at a time. You call it, Do or Don't, and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it. {name}, you're the scorekeeper.

As you play, keep John Doe's BCRC check in mind. His age rules out the 65-plus trigger, but something is still left to verify, and the file has to show it was checked.
