why.say:
Quick one, true or false? Getting your plan sent back with comments means you did a bad job.

{name}, true or false? Hands up for true. Okay, every hand that went up, put it down, because it's false.

Here's the thing. A plan sitting in draft does nobody any good. It only works once Atty. Thorne has seen it and the file runs on an approved version.

That step of sending it to him is called routing, and it's where your work becomes approved work. So routing isn't paperwork.

Yes, your plan will sit in an attorney's review queue, and yes, some days that queue moves at the speed of a Monday morning. It still beats a plan nobody ever saw. And being sent back is the system working.

I once trained someone so scared of getting comments that she quietly left the scariest risk off her plan. Guess which risk the adjuster found first? Yep.

By the end of this, you'll know the one move that keeps that from ever happening to you.
why.ask: {name}, how would you feel if your first plan came back with comments, and what would you do next?

theory.say:
A Case Plan is a living document. You draft it, Atty. Thorne reviews it, and then the file runs on it.

Every plan uses the same section templates, which just means the same headings in the same order, so a reviewer can scan it fast and nothing gets missed.

The review loop goes draft, route, review, approve, run, and a return is just a normal step back to draft.

Then there's the pre-confirmation stage: a conclusion that's still waiting on its proof. If the proof shows up different, the plan goes back for review.

And here's the part I really want you to hear. The CMS keeps every version, untouched, and every note you write is discoverable, meaning the other side can ask to see it in a lawsuit.

{name}, imagine your note read out loud in a deposition. Still happy with it?
theory.ask: {name}, if every note is discoverable, how should that change the way you write a treatment note?

frame.say:
Four things you track to stay compliant, and I'll tell you at the end which one trips people up most.

First, record integrity. The CMS keeps a history of every version nobody can change, so nothing gets quietly edited.

Second, state deadlines. In some states the insurance company can demand an early IME, which is an exam by a doctor they pick, and that date goes on the calendar. Not in your head, which on a busy Monday has about as much storage as a flip phone.

Set two reminders, because the first one gets snoozed and the second one gets snoozed harder.

Third, Letters of Protection, or LOPs. That's a letter where a doctor agrees to wait for payment until the case settles. You need to know which providers are treating that way, so no bill shows up as a surprise.

And fourth, the Golden Rule: the medical plan and the legal claim run side by side. Coordinate them, but never mix them.

That fourth one is the trip wire. {name}, why do you think mixing them is so dangerous?
frame.ask: {name}, what does “coordinate, don't mix” look like in one sentence of a real treatment note?

rules.say:
Now the rules. Draft in the section templates, not your own made-up layout. Put each task's owner and date in their own fields, not buried in a sentence.

Route for review before you do anything that speaks for the firm outside the office. When a plan comes back, answer every comment and re-route. Never run a plan that's half fixed.

Record the approved version, because the file runs on the approved plan, not your latest draft. And when an important fact changes, re-route.

Compare two notes. "Updated the plan, it's fine." Versus "Marked version two superseded, drafted version three with the new fact, routed to Atty. Thorne at 2:15."

Notice the second one never says "per my last email." The version history says that for you, politely. And it's the one that holds up when someone asks what you knew and when.

Keep notes clean and factual, legal strategy only in the legal track, and legal questions go to Atty. Thorne.
rules.ask: {name}, right now, which version of the plan is John Doe's file running against?

model.say:
Look at this picture. Before I explain it, {name}, find me the one thing on the right that's orange. Got it? Hold on to that.

On the left is the editor, laid out like a page, with four numbered callouts: the section templates, the risks band, the owner and date fields, and the route-for-review button.

On the right, the routing loop as a closed circle: draft, route, review, approved, run.

And there's the orange branch, returned with comment, running back to draft. It's drawn just as bold as the approval branch, on purpose. Sending back is normal, not a failure.

Underneath it all runs a thin grey bar, the audit trail, which is the history of every version ever saved.

Plenty of Case Managers try to dodge that orange arrow. The great ones expect it and plan for it.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think the return branch is drawn as boldly as the approval branch?

job.say:
Let's follow one plan through its life. You've drafted all five bands, so you hit route for review, and the CMS stamps the time.

It comes back with comments. You fix every single one under Revisions and re-route.

Then, after it's approved, a big fact changes. The tempting move is to open the approved plan and just type over it. Please don't.

I've seen that exact move turn a deposition into an hour of "So what did the plan say before you changed it?"

Instead, mark it superseded under Version and route a new one, so the old version is kept and the new one goes to Atty. Thorne.

Why does it matter? Because a clean version history tells the adjuster this firm knows exactly what it knew and when.

{name}, here's your challenge: what fact on John Doe's file do you think will force the first re-route?
job.ask: {name}, if a fact changes after approval, what's the very first button you click?

dodont.say:
Game time: three clues, one rule. Each round hides one of this lesson's do's or don'ts about routing and record-keeping.

I'll give you three clues, one at a time. Shout do or don't and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it.

{name}, you're captain of the left side of the room, and you're captain of the right, {name}.

Keep John Doe's file in mind. The gap investigation on Day 3 is going to change the picture and force a re-route, so knowing how to supersede a plan really matters.

And one warning, out loud. Defense lawyers love opinions in medical notes. They use them to argue the Case Manager wasn't neutral. Facts only, every time.

Final mystery: one line already in John Doe's file could become a problem in a deposition. Who can find it first?
dodont.ask: {name}, which do or don't do you think gets broken most on a busy Friday afternoon?

case.say:
Before I show you what just landed, a quick game: two truths and a lie. One, Cardinal State has an adjuster assigned. Two, Leah Moran accepted Property Damage liability this morning. Three, John Doe hasn't started treatment. {name}, which is the lie?

Okay, the reveal. It's 02/17/2026, and a message from Atty. Thorne just landed: letters of representation go out today.

Where the claims stand: Keystone BI, KM-26-440871, with Dana Whitfield, and Keystone PD with Leah Moran, who did accept PD liability this morning. Harbor Point, HP-26-7741, with Marcus Bell, for Host UM and PIP. And Cardinal State, CS-26-20355, with no adjuster yet. That's the lie.

He wants the three LORs, plus notices to Bluewater and Peach State, on his desk for signature today. Preferred delivery methods are in the Communications Log.

In real life, “on his desk today” means before the one person who signs everything disappears to lunch. Letters that need a signature can sense lunchtime.

{name}, you've got the claim numbers and the call log. That's all you need.

Five letters, one signature, today.
case.ask: {name}, before you draft a word, which two letters do you think need the most care, and why?

task.say:
Here's the job. Generate John Doe's full letter set on the firm template in CMS Documents, under Outgoing.

That's LORs to Keystone for BI with the Property Damage carve-out, to Harbor Point for Host UM and PIP, and to Cardinal State for Relative UM, plus notices to Bluewater and Peach State Health Plan.

Give each the right Attn line, insured, claim, policy or member number, and the date of loss, with requests for limits, Declaration Pages, any other coverage and preservation.

Route the set to Atty. Thorne for signature, send each the way that company prefers from the Email Workspace, and calendar the acknowledgement checks.

Where I'm grading your judgment: what Keystone's letter leaves out, and why no UM letter asks for money. {name}, you've got Keystone. {name}, you've got the two UM letters, and you'll explain your choices to the room.

Think of Keystone like a neighbor with a perfect memory. Everything we tell Keystone, Keystone remembers forever.

Five letters sent is the floor. Five letters that each give that insurer exactly what it needs, and not one word more, is the job.
task.ask: {name}, what goes in the Attn line for Cardinal State, and why not a name?

check.say:
Check your set before you log it. {name}, count with me: LORs to Keystone, Harbor Point and Cardinal State, notices to Bluewater and Peach State. Five.

Attn lines: Dana Whitfield, Marcus Bell, and “Attn: Claims Department” for Cardinal State.

Now the insured lines, and look closely, because these get swapped all the time: Robert Smith, Kevin Alvarez, Margaret Doe, and Margaret Doe again on Bluewater, because the Civic and its policy are hers.

Subject lines carry the claim number and 02/06/2026; Peach State's carries PSH-55017742 and GRP-41208. Keystone gets his name only, with the carve-out limited to the Civic and 5 business days to inspect.

Neither UM letter asks for money. Bluewater's asks for the signed rejection form from 03/14/2024. John Doe's told to preserve the doorbell-camera video.

Every letter went to Atty. Thorne for signature, sent 02/17/2026, with a follow-up on 02/20/2026. A letter he didn't sign fails, however beautiful it is.

Mystery for later: one of these letters will get its answer a full month after the others. Which one would you bet on?
check.ask: {name}, on your Harbor Point and Cardinal State letters, whose name is in the insured line, and why that person?

case.say: Quick warm-up. I'm going to read three numbers, and you shout which one pays first: $20,000, $10,000, $10,000. {name}, go. Interesting. Hold that answer. It's the morning of 02/17/2026, and the letters haven't gone out yet. All three insurance companies opened claims by phone on 02/16 and 02/17 and told us their limits on those set-up calls: Keystone Mutual's BI, Harbor Point's Host UM, and Cardinal State's Relative UM, with no adjuster assigned there yet. Here's the catch: nothing is confirmed in writing. Today's LORs will ask each one for its Declaration Page, and Keystone will want John Doe's signed authorizations first. Nothing's been entered in the Insurance tab yet, and the letters can't pull the insurance details until it is. Now the reveal. Say the order with me, bottom-up: BI pays first, and only once it's used up does Host UM open. So the $10,000 BI pays first, even though it's the smallest. {name}, did you get it?
case.ask: {name}, before any letter goes out, is the $10,000 BI limit confirmed, or still preliminary?

task.say: Here's your job. You're building the complete Policy Stack for John Doe v. Robert Smith in the CMS Insurance tab. Enter all three layers in the order they pay, with the insurer, policy number, claim number, limit and adjuster for each, and mark each one first-party or third-party. In the Comments box, write the insurer's actual name, the driver's name where it's different from the owner's, and the adjuster's details, or say plainly that none is assigned yet. Then check the total, record the order the layers must be pursued in, and mark the projection preliminary, meaning it's a forecast and not a promise, until every limit's confirmed in writing. Please don't enter these as three equal claims. UM owes nothing until BI is used up. {name}, you're entering BI. {name}, you're on the two UM layers. And I promise at least one of these insurers will ask you to spell “Doe.” Twice. The lazy stack is three numbers in boxes. The high-value stack tells Atty. Thorne the order, the source, and what's still a guess.
task.ask: {name}, what could happen if the BI claim were settled without the UM insurers' written consent?

model.say: Here's the stack drawn as a ladder, built from the bottom up so you can feel the order. Rung one at the bottom, in navy: BI, $10,000. Rung two: Host UM, $20,000. Rung three at the top, in orange: Relative UM, $10,000. Each rung carries its insurer, claim number and adjuster in small type on the right. Along the right side, an orange brace spans all three rungs with the total set large: $40,000. And underneath, a card headed verify each layer, with one empty checkbox per layer. The rungs are numbered one, two, three, bottom to top, and they're never reordered. I once watched a new Case Manager arrange a stack biggest number first, because, and I quote, “it looks more impressive.” It did look impressive. It was also completely wrong. {name}, why does the order matter more than the size?
model.ask: {name}, whose policy is the Host UM, and how does John Doe get to reach it?

check.say: Let's check the stack before you log it, and I'm calling on people. {name}, are all three layers there, BI, Host UM and Relative UM, with limits of $10,000, $20,000 and $10,000, adding up to $40,000? Is the order recorded as BI, then Host UM, then Relative UM? BI marked third-party, both UM layers first-party? Policy and claim numbers filled in for every layer, and the Relative UM adjuster recorded as “No adjuster assigned yet,” not left blank? The source of each limit noted, the set-up call for now, with the Declaration Page to be requested in the LOR? And the projection marked preliminary? Don't predict value before coverage is confirmed, and don't quote a likely limit to the client. Clients hear a number once and it gets tattooed on their brain. Lazy check: the total's right. High-value check: the total's right and I can prove where every number came from. Here's your mystery for the letters: one layer will need something signed by John Doe before it tells us anything at all.
check.ask: {name}, if your total isn't $40,000, which rung is in the wrong place?

case.say:
Game first: guess the number. I tell you a total on a chart, you guess how many mistakes are hiding behind it. Ready? $45,000. {name}, your guess? {name}, higher or lower? Not telling.

Here's what landed. It's 03/11/2026. A colleague has been keeping John Doe's Coverage Matrix, and the CMS has flagged it.

The Keystone BI follow-up for the Declaration Page was due 03/05/2026, and nothing's logged. The total reads $45,000, while the Case Plan says $40,000.

Since the matrix was last edited, new documents arrived: Harbor Point's letter of 03/02/2026, Cardinal State's adjuster assignment on 03/03/2026, and its Coverage Letter on 03/09/2026.

Keystone's written request with the signed authorizations went out, but no Declaration Page yet. And this morning Summit Imaging asked for a Letter of Protection, which was declined because PIP pays first.

You've got the matrix and the documents. It's a spot-the-difference puzzle, except every difference is somebody's money.

A total is only as true as the rows under it.
case.ask: {name}, what's the first thing you'd check when a stack total reads $45,000 instead of $40,000?

task.say:
Here's the job. Audit the matrix against the documents in CMS Documents. Find every error, fix it, and cite the document and date that prove each fix.

Restore the stack total, clear every overdue follow-up by actually doing it and setting a new date, and leave the correct rows alone.

Then a live call in the Call Simulator with Dana Whitfield at Keystone. Confirm she has the written request and the signed authorizations, get a firm date for the Declaration Page in writing, share no treatment details and no demand figure. Then log the call and set the next follow-up by 03/13/2026.

Finally, send a three-line audit note to Atty. Thorne: confirmed in writing, still preliminary, escalated.

{name}, you're making the Keystone call. {name}, you're listening for anything she gets out of you that she shouldn't, and you'll tell us what it was.

Expect to hear “I'll have to check on that.” Your job is to turn that into a date.

“She'll get back to me” isn't an outcome. A date in writing is.
task.ask: {name}, on 03/11/2026, what status can you honestly give the BI row, and why?

model.say:
This is the matrix exactly as you found it on 03/11/2026. A full-width CMS table with a navy header and six rows, deliberately imperfect.

A navy rail on the left marks the stack rows, and PIP is sitting inside it, wrongly, as row four. A grey divider separates the rows that belong outside the stack. At the bottom, the total in large type: $45,000.

When we reveal the answers, red rings appear on the planted errors, the total gets struck through with $40,000 beside it, and PIP drops below the divider.

On the right is the audit-note card to Atty. Elijah Thorne, three lines: confirmed in writing, preliminary, escalated.

Here's the thing about a wrong total: it never looks wrong. $45,000 looks just as confident as $40,000. Like a bathroom scale that's off by five pounds, it tells you nothing until you check it.

{name}, before the reveal, I want your eyes on that navy rail.

Check the rows, not the bottom line.
model.ask: {name}, without the reveal, what tells you PIP doesn't belong on that navy rail?

check.say:
Check your audit before you log it. BI should read preliminary, verbal from the set-up call, written request sent, because Keystone's Declaration Page doesn't arrive until 03/20/2026.

The 03/05/2026 follow-up was overdue, so you called Dana Whitfield on 03/11/2026, logged it, and set the next date by 03/13/2026.

Host UM's form is add-on, from Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter. Teresa Okafor replaces “not yet assigned.” PIP moved out of the stack, and the total corrected from $45,000 to $40,000.

Bluewater's “UM: none” needs the signed rejection form from 03/14/2024 chased. Keystone's PD row stays outside the stack, marked preliminary; moving it in or deleting it is a false alarm. Finding Cardinal State's unstated form and its excess clause earns extra credit.

Every fix cites a document. {name}, read us your audit note the way Atty. Thorne would read it, in ten seconds, between two meetings.

Mystery to chew on: Keystone's Declaration Page finally lands on 03/20/2026. Which line on it will you read first, and what changes on the matrix the same day?
check.ask: {name}, in ten seconds, does your audit note tell Atty. Thorne what he must decide?

case.say: This one runs on two dates. On 03/12/2026 Dion Carver at Peach State Health Plan writes about member PSH-55017742, recovery file SRU-26-03318: following the plan's 02/27/2026 notice, it's processing John Doe's accident-related claims and will assert reimbursement from any recovery. No lien record exists on the matter yet. Then on 06/10/2026 the plan's interim itemization arrives, and it asserts $3,618.00 across five claim lines. The pre-demand audit is still ahead of us, so whatever figure we accept now is the figure the demand and the Net Sheet will carry.
case.ask: {name}, if you typed $3,618.00 into the lien register today, who would that cost?

task.say: On 03/12/2026 you register Peach State's claim in CMS Liens and flag it against the matter: carrier, member ID and group number, its place in the Payer Order, the basis it asserts, and the date of the flag, with the Triple-Check results beside it. Say that date out loud when you set it. Then you answer Dion Carver in the Email Workspace, noting the claim and asking for an itemized ledger once anything is paid. On 06/10/2026 you audit that ledger line by line, send the dispute, get the corrected balance confirmed in writing, and file the exchange in the CMS and on the Backup Drive. And in one line, tell me what has to happen before this lien can be compromised.
task.ask: {name}, what's the date you're setting on that flag, and why that day?

audit.say: Here is Peach State's interim itemization, and I want a call on every line. A plan's recovery vendor pulls every claim from the coverage date, so you'll find a 02/03/2026 eye exam from before the collision, a sinus infection on 03/18/2026, and an allergy visit on 05/06/2026 for a condition he already had. The Crescent injection is the subtle one: the paid column says $1,860.00, but the plan is claiming the billed $3,400.00. Summit's MRI is fine at $0.00, because PIP paid it. And the cover letter wants full repayment with no reduction, which is not yours to answer. These results come back in minutes here; on a real file a corrected itemization takes weeks.
audit.ask: {name}, which number on the Crescent line may a Health Plan claim, and why?

check.say: Run your record against this before you log it. Peach State is the carrier, with PSH-55017742 and GRP-41208 both entered. Its position sits after PIP and before the LOP providers. The three unrelated lines are disputed and Crescent is at the $1,860.00 the plan paid. The flag is dated before any demand is drafted. And the $1,860.00 is confirmed in writing on 06/24/2026, with any compromise left to Atty. Thorne. When Dion Carver asked whether John would repay in full and what the limits were, the right answer acknowledged the figure, honored the notice and routed the rest. Registering a lien isn't conceding it; the lien stage is where it gets reduced.
check.ask: {name}, reading your record cold at the lien stage, what would a negotiator still have to go looking for?

case.say: Quick game first. Hands up if you've ever put off going to the doctor because you were busy. Keep them up if it was more than a week. Look around: half the room. Now hold that thought, because an insurance adjuster thinks every one of you was faking. Here's what just landed. On 03/13/2026, a CMS notice: Riverton Urgent Care's 02/20/2026 note and Riverton Spine & Rehab's visits since 02/24/2026 are now on the treatment timeline, right beside the 02/06/2026 EMS Run Report. {name}, the crash was 02/06/2026. When was John Doe first seen? Count it out loud. Fourteen days. That's what we call a Treatment Gap, which just means days where an injured person got no care at all. Now read the last line of the notice. Risk Flags: none recorded. Nobody has caught it. Not the system, and not the adjuster, whose out-of-office reply has said "back Monday" since February. Everything we do on Days 3 to 5 leans on this flag existing and being right, and today, it's yours.
case.ask: {name}, before you call John Doe, what documents could show where he was and what he was doing in those fourteen days?

task.say: Here's your job. Flag the Treatment Gap in two places: the Risk Flags in the Case File, and the risks band of the Action Plan Editor, which is just the section of the plan where we list everything that could hurt the case. Compute it exactly. The lazy flag says "about two weeks." The high-value flag says 02/06/2026 to 02/20/2026, fourteen days, and sets a watch for any later break in care. Then list the likely causes you'll look into, the steps you need before the gap can be explained, and route the flag to Atty. Thorne. I had a Case Manager once who wrote "client seemed busy" as the reason for a gap. The adjuster quoted that line back to us in the offer letter. We spent a month digging out of three words. {name}, you're up first: what's the exact date range you're typing in?
task.ask: {name}, give me three likely reasons a client goes two weeks before seeing anyone, without guessing for him?

check.say: Before you log it, let's check it like the adjuster would. {name}, read me your gap. It should say fourteen days, 02/06/2026 to 02/20/2026, not "about two weeks." Is a watch set for the next break in care, so each one gets documented the same way? The risks band holds facts only: the dates, the length, and a note that John Doe's own explanation and the papers behind it are still to come. Nothing about what the gap will do to the claim; that's Atty. Thorne's call. Your investigation steps are listed, his own account first, then work schedules, appointment records, anything in writing. And it's routed to Atty. Thorne. Here's why I'm this picky. When an adjuster finds a gap before we do, we don't get a phone call. We get a very polite email, and then a lower offer. Adjusters cut offers on gaps all the time, and a gap we flagged and explained early hurts far less than one they find first. So, your mystery: something kept John Doe out of care for fourteen days. Tomorrow we find out what. {name}, what's your best guess?
check.ask: {name}, did you set a watch for the next break in care, and where will it show up?

case.say: Little guessing game. {name}, how many questions do you think Atty. Thorne should have to ask you after reading your Case Plan? Shout a number. The answer is zero, and that's the whole activity. This is the gate out of Claim Set Up, not a wrap-up. Everything is in the file: parties mapped, the $40,000 stack verified, the onboarding packet delivered and tracked, and the 14-day Treatment Gap flagged. The stack, by the way, is just the layers of insurance stacked up to pay this claim. And on 03/16/2026, this lands from Atty. Thorne: he needs the full Case Plan on John Doe, all five bands, routed to him by end of day. The acceptance decision and why, the stack in order with a rough early estimate, liability, the triple-check on privacy, Medicare and who pays first held open, the three pillars, clinical, functional and financial, with owners and dates, and the risks band. Docket the filing window. If he has to ask, it isn't finished.
case.ask: {name}, what's one thing that would make Atty. Thorne come back to you with a question?

task.say: You're drafting the complete Case Plan for John Doe v. Robert Smith in the Action Plan Editor. All five bands. The acceptance decision with its reason. Coverage as a stack, in the order it pays, plus liability, which just means who's at fault, and an early projection. The triple-check, held open until the Treatment Phase. Clinical, Functional and Financial pillars with goals you can measure, every task with an owner and a date. And the risks band, with the 14-day gap and the risk of a later break in care, right up front. Docket the filing window, then route it. Lazy plans say "follow up with doctor." Great plans say "Call Riverton Spine & Rehab for visit notes, owner me, due Friday." "Follow up with doctor" is how a task sits on your list so long it starts asking for its own desk. And here's a hint: the route button stays locked until every band is complete. {name}, if you can't route, that's the plan telling you something.
task.ask: {name}, if your route button is still locked, which band do you think is incomplete?

check.say: Read your plan like Atty. Thorne will. {name}, read me your snapshot: parties, 02/06/2026, statute of limitations 02/06/2028, which is the deadline to file the lawsuit, and the client as a passenger. Acceptance decision with its reason. Coverage at $10,000, $20,000 and $10,000, total $40,000, in order: BI, the other driver's policy, then Host UM, from the car John rode in, then Relative UM, from his household relative's policy, with the projection marked preliminary and no number promised before coverage is confirmed. Liability preliminary until the Police Report and driver statements back it up. Triple-check held open. Every task with an owner and a date. Gap up front. Plan routed with a timestamp. And if Atty. Thorne does ask you something, the answer can't be "I'll have to check with my supervisor." On this file, you are the one who knows. Now the gate, the four things done before the file moves on: LORs out and logged, stack verified at $40,000, gap flagged, plan routed. All four, or the Treatment Phase doesn't start. Every one of those touches the final settlement number. I once saw a whole demand delayed a month because one LOR was never logged. Nobody knew it was missing.
check.ask: {name}, could Atty. Thorne set strategy from your plan without asking you a single question?

questions.say: Welcome to the Learning Check, game-show edition. You answer from John Doe's file, in your own words, typed under each question, and I'll call a few of you up to defend your answers live. Question one, for the warm-up: name the six stages of John Doe's file in order, and tell me what the Case Manager owns at Intake and Case Opening that nobody else will. Question two, the tricky one: John Doe asks you two things on one call, what his case is worth, and whether waiting to see a doctor hurt it. Word for word, what do you tell him on each, who answers if you don't, and what do you record and route? Question three, the big-money question: you're opening his matter in the CMS. What has to happen before the matter is created, on whose names, and why does the order matter? {name}, you're up first when the timer ends. If your mind goes blank, that's normal. On my first Learning Check, I spelled my own name wrong. {name}, you're defending question two.
questions.ask: {name}, before you type: which of the three questions are you most nervous about, and why?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary. Write the principles in your own words, not the clicks. Then think through this scenario. Robert Smith's insurance company has already called John Doe, all friendly, and he needs a car to get to work. What do you tell him today, in what order, and what has to be on the file before tomorrow's claim set-up? Real talk: I once had a client give a Recorded Statement, a taped interview the adjuster can quote forever, to the other side's adjuster because they "sounded really nice." He said he felt "pretty much fine" the day after the crash. That one sentence followed us all the way to settlement. The right answer puts things on the record and sends anything about value or fault to Atty. Thorne. {name}, you'll share yours first.
summary.ask: {name}, what's the very first thing you'd tell John when he mentions the carrier's call?

scale.say: Last one, the Skill Scale. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each skill, then submit for review. I'll put your self-rating next to your score, and where there's a big gap, we'll talk. Honest beats impressive here. And no, "I submitted it, the system ate it" won't work. If it isn't in the CMS, it didn't happen, and that includes your homework. One more thing: UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach. And here's your mystery to sleep on. John Doe's file is open, the stack is $40,000, and he was a passenger. But tomorrow, he might go quiet on us. If your client stops answering the phone, what's the first thing you do, and what's the last? {name}, I want your answer first thing next block.
scale.ask: {name}, where do you honestly sit, 1 to 5, on opening a matter correctly in the CMS?

questions.say: Welcome to the Learning Check, lightning-round style. I'll read each question, and before you type, I'm picking one person to shout a five-word headline answer, then everyone writes the full version in their own words from John Doe's file. {name}, you're up for question one. First, name every coverage on the file, whose it is and what it pays, then tell me which three make the $40,000 Recovery Stack and why the others stay out. Second, before the letters went out you built the Policy Stack in the CMS: give each layer's insurer, claim number, limit, first- or third-party, and the order it's pursued in. {name}, you've got the headline on that one. Third, list the five letters that left the file on 02/17/2026, with the insured each one named and how it was addressed. For every “confirmed,” give me the document behind it. No answer like “the adjuster said so on the phone.” Adjusters say a lot of things on the phone.
questions.ask: {name}, five-word headline: which three coverages make the $40,000, and which famous one doesn't?

summary.say: Time for your Self-Summary: the principles in your own words. Then work the scenario. It's 03/11/2026. Keystone still hasn't confirmed its limit in writing, and John Doe started treatment fourteen days after the crash. Which three actions do you take today, in what order, and what goes in the Case Plan's risks section? As you write, think about what you would say, and not say, to an insurance company that calls you about this file today. Here's a story to keep you honest. I once had a Case Manager tell an adjuster, trying to sound on top of things, “Oh, he's been treating the whole time.” He hadn't. That one friendly sentence turned into the adjuster's favorite quote in the whole negotiation. Facts only, and only the ones they're entitled to. {name}, while you write, I'll be coming around to read the first line of yours.
summary.ask: {name}, if Dana Whitfield called you today asking about the gap, what would you tell her?

scale.say: Last part, the Skill Scale. Rate each skill 1 to 5 and submit it for review. When the scores come back, I'll compare your self-rating with your score. A 5 sitting next to a $45,000 stack is a coaching conversation, and we'll have it, nicely. Remember the legal line works like a gate: a great score doesn't survive a letter signed for the attorney, or a coverage opinion given to an insurer or the client. Rating yourself, by the way, is a lot like a client describing their policy: everybody thinks they have full coverage until somebody reads the fine print. Be honest; an honest 3 helps me more than a hopeful 5. Now your mystery for what's next. We've got a $40,000 stack, letters out, matrix clean. But there's one thing on this file that could make every one of those insurers offer less, and it has nothing to do with coverage. {name}, I want your guess before we move on.
scale.ask: {name}, what on this file, besides coverage, could make every insurer offer less?

questions.say: Welcome to the game show. Today's category is Claim Set Up, and the prize is bragging rights for the rest of the week. Here's how it works: you answer from the file, in your own words, typed under each question, and then I'll pull a few contestants up to read theirs. Question one: lay out the five bands of the Case Plan and what goes in each, including the three pillars: clinical, functional and financial, or body, life and money. Question two: explain why a bad fact buried in the middle of a plan hasn't really been told to Atty. Thorne at all. Question three: state John Doe's coverage exactly as it belongs in the plan, the layers, limits, total, the order they pay in, and where the projection stands. {name}, you're my first contestant on question two. {name}, you've got question three. No pressure, but the whole room is your studio audience. Coffee refills are allowed between questions. I'm a Case Manager, not a monster.
questions.ask: {name}, if you had to bury one bad fact so nobody noticed, where would you hide it, and why is that exactly the wrong instinct?

summary.say: Now the Self-Summary, in your own words. And one last scenario for the day. It's 03/11/2026. Keystone still hasn't confirmed its limit in writing, and John Doe started treatment fourteen days after the crash. {name}, what three things do you do today, in what order, and what goes in the risks band? Here's a war story to help. I had a Case Manager who took a carrier's word on the phone that the limit was what we thought. Never got it in writing. Months later, a different adjuster said the policy was smaller. Guess who had nothing to prove it? The only thing on the calendar for that limit was a reminder that said "get it in writing," snoozed eleven times. The plan is the foundation for everything that comes next. Every bill and every lien check in the Treatment Phase reads from the stack you verified today. Get it wrong now, and every number after it is wrong too.
summary.ask: {name}, if an approved plan changes after a new fact arrives, do you edit it or re-route it?

scale.say: Last thing for Claim Set Up: the Skill Scale. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each skill, then submit it. I'll compare your ratings with your scores across Intake and Claim Set Up, and we'll talk about any big gaps. Before anyone heads to the Treatment Phase, let's say the gate out loud together: LORs, the talk-to-our-lawyer letters, out and logged, the three-layer stack of BI, Host UM and Relative UM verified at $40,000, the gap flagged, plan routed. Now, your mystery. We have three insurance companies on this claim, and one of them still hasn't put its limit in writing. Our letters asked every carrier to commit, and in the Treatment Phase we start chasing John Doe's care while we wait. {name}, here's your homework question: if Keystone comes back with a smaller number than we expect, what happens to that $40,000, and who do you tell first?
scale.ask: {name}, looking at the four gate items, which one are you least confident you've truly cleared?

why.say: Quick game: Fact or Opinion. I'll say a sentence a Case Manager might say to a client. Thumbs up if it's a fact, thumbs down if it's an opinion. Ready? "Your appointment is Tuesday at ten." "You'll probably get the policy limits." "We sent the letter on Friday." "Don't worry, the gap won't matter." {name}, you were the only one up on that last one. Tell us why. Here's the thing. That last one sounds kind, doesn't it? That's exactly why it's dangerous. Today we're drawing the UPL line. UPL is the unauthorized practice of law, which in plain words means giving legal advice without a law license. It almost never happens on purpose. It happens when a worried client asks a kind Case Manager a question, and the Case Manager tries to help. And half the time, the client thinks we're the insurance company anyway. I once had a client ask me, very politely, to just mail his check to his cousin's house. So here's a simple rule, and one sentence that will save you every time.
why.ask: {name}, has anyone ever asked you for an opinion at work that you weren't sure you were allowed to give?

theory.say: Four ideas, all practical. Fact sharing is telling John Doe what a record says: a date, an amount, what was sent and when. Process explanation is telling him what happens next, what a form is for, and who decides, but never how it ends. Legal advice is any opinion on what his facts mean for his rights, his money or his choices, and that belongs to Atty. Thorne alone. And the habit that keeps you safe, the sentence I promised you, is hear, log, route. You write his question down word for word and send it to Atty. Thorne the same day. The lazy version is "Uh, I'm not sure, call back later." The high-value version is "Great question, that one's for Atty. Thorne. I've written it down exactly, and you'll hear from him by Friday." Same rule, totally different client experience. {name}, which one would you rather hear if you were hurt and scared?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these four do you think is hardest to hold onto on a busy day?

rules.say: The rules, in plain words. Legal advice is any opinion on what John Doe's facts mean. You can share facts: dates, documents, what was sent and when. You can explain the process: what happens next, and who decides. You never give an opinion on what the case is worth, on strategy, on whether to settle, or on what a fact like a gap in treatment does to the money. When he asks, you hear it, log it word for word, route it to Atty. Thorne the same day, and tell him when to expect an answer. One test before you speak: am I telling him what is, or what it means? "What is" is yours. Why does this matter so much? Because if you guess a number and you're wrong, the client anchors on it. Every honest offer after that feels like an insult, and good settlements get turned down over one sentence you said to be nice.
rules.ask: {name}, John Doe says, “Just tell me honestly, is my case any good?” What's your exact answer?

model.say: Same questions, answered two ways. Before I reveal the right side, {name}, guess which column has the friendliest-sounding answers. Hold that. On the left, fact sharing. "The Police Report lists the date of loss as 02/06/2026." "The next step is a letter to each insurance company saying we represent you." "That's a question for Atty. Thorne; I've logged it, and he'll call you by Friday." On the right, the versions that cross the line. "Your case is probably worth the policy limits." "I'd take the offer." "The gap will hurt your case." "Don't worry, it won't matter." And there's the reveal. The kind ones are on the right too. Comfort about the outcome is still an opinion on his case. A Case Manager I trained once told a client, "Relax, you've basically already won." The client quit physical therapy that week. Why go, if he'd already won?
model.ask: {name}, which answer on the right sounds the most harmless, and why is it still advice?

job.say: Here's a normal day. John Doe calls and asks what his case is worth. That's Atty. Thorne's question. You log his words exactly in Case Notes, open a task, and it's routed before you go home, with no number given. He asks what happens next, and that one's yours: you explain the next step in plain words, with no prediction of how it ends. And when an adjuster or a doctor's office asks what you think of the case, you decline politely, share only facts the firm has approved, and log the contact in the Communications Log. And when a client calls to file a claim with you guys, kindly explain that we're his law firm, not his insurance company. The insurance company is the one we're politely arguing with. Once an adjuster called and said, all friendly, "Off the record, what do you think this one's worth?" There's no off the record with an adjuster. Anything you say becomes their opening offer. {name}, what would you say to that adjuster?
job.ask: {name}, an adjuster says, “Off the record, what's your number?” What do you say back?

dodont.say: Let's play 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides a Do or a Don't about the UPL line. Three clues, one at a time. Call it the moment you know, Do or Don't, and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it. {name}, you're team captain on the left. {name}, you've got the right. As you play, listen for the kind answers. The ones that sound caring are often the ones that cross the line. The bare-minimum Case Manager either stonewalls the client or comforts them with a guess. The high-value one gives a clear process and a time frame for Atty. Thorne's answer. That's the safe kindness. Now your challenge for the next block: when we open John Doe's raw file, there's a question he already asked at intake that nobody routed. Find it, and tell me who should have heard about it.
dodont.ask: {name}, what's the one sentence you'll say every time a client asks what their case is worth?

why.say: Let's play Two Truths and a Lie, John Doe edition. I'll tell you three things about him, and you vote on which one is fake. One: he owns his own car. Two: he started a new job last month. Three: he declined the ambulance after the crash. Hands up for one. Two. Three. {name}, you're voting with the crowd or against it? The lie is number one. John Doe doesn't own a car, and that one little fact might be the most important thing in this whole block. Here's why. Assessment is more than reading medical records. And back at intake, on 02/09/2026, there weren't any medical records. There's the EMS Run Report, the ambulance crew's write-up, which says restrained front-seat passenger, neck stiffness, declined transport. And there's John himself. If our plan only treats the chart, it misses what actually stops people from getting care: no ride, a new job he's scared to miss, a worry about who pays. That's how a Treatment Gap is born.
why.ask: {name}, what could stop John Doe from getting to a first appointment this week?

theory.say: The assessment has four areas, and I want you to guess which one new Case Managers skip. First is Clinical Evaluation: his physical, thinking and emotional problems, written down the way he tells them and the way the records show them. We never diagnose. Second is Social Determinants, a fancy phrase for his life outside the doctor's office: housing, family support, money. John lives with his mother, Margaret Doe, he owns no car, and her Civic was damaged in the crash. Third is Pre-Morbid Status, which just means how he was before the crash. It's what separates an old problem from a new injury, and nothing's on file for it yet. Fourth is the Vocational Outlook: can he go back to his job, or will he need retraining? He's a warehouse shift lead at Northgate Distribution, on 8-hour shifts at $22.00 an hour. {name}, which one did you guess? Most people skip the social one, and it's usually the one that causes the gap.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these four areas would you be tempted to skip on a busy intake day?

theory2.say: Once you know the person, you set goals and map out the care. Every goal has to hold up in front of a doctor and an adjuster, so each one carries a real measurement and a date. Then the Care Coordination Strategy sorts the treatment into four groups. Acute and restorative care, like surgery, physical therapy and occupational therapy, which helps people get back to everyday tasks. Psychological support, like counseling or CBT, a type of talk therapy. Durable medical equipment, which is gear like wheelchairs, ramps or braces. And rehabilitation milestones, the move from hospital care, to outpatient visits, to care at home. John declined transport, so his care would start as outpatient. Here's the thing nobody tells you: every one of those moves between stages is a trapdoor where a gap can open. That's why each one goes on the calendar. {name}, I'm going to make you guess the forgotten group.
theory2.ask: {name}, which of the four groups do you think gets forgotten most often on injury files?

frame.say: Here's the SMART table, and I'll show you a bad goal and a great one. Specific means naming the actual task. Bad: "improve mobility." Great: "walk 50 meters with a rolling walker." Measurable means a standard scale an adjuster can check: range of motion, which is how far a joint can move, a pain or disability score, or sessions attended. Achievable means realistic for his recovery, and the doctor's outlook decides that, never the claim. Relevant means tied to the injuries we're claiming, to his daily life, and to getting back to work. A goal that needs therapy at 10 a.m. three days a week for a man on 8-hour shifts isn't a goal, it's a wish. Time-bound means a check-in date, like by the 12-week review. Now, who owns what? The doctor sets the medical target and the measurement. We write the goal in plain words into the Case Plan. I once read a goal that said "client will feel better soon." The adjuster wrote back one word: "Measured how?" {name}, you get to fix John's goal.
frame.ask: {name}, how would you turn “help John get back to work” into a SMART goal?

rules.say: Let's put the rules together, and I'll show you the bare-minimum version first. The lazy assessment says "neck pain, follow up." Done. The high-value assessment looks at the whole person. On this file that started with the intake call and the Run Report. You write medical findings in his words and the record's words, never your own diagnosis. You dig into his life: who he lives with, how he'll get to care, whether cost is holding him back. You ask about every old injury, treatment and claim, with dates and doctors, and you request those records yourself. Why? Because if the defense finds an old back injury before we do, it looks like we were hiding it, and that can knock real money off a settlement. You write down what his job asks of his body. Then you build SMART goals the doctor confirms, map the four care groups, and calendar every risk before it turns into a gap. The plan coordinates care. It never prescribes it.
rules.ask: {name}, if a client mentions an old back injury, what do you write down, and what don't you write?

model.say: Remember the mystery from the last block, what's stopping John Doe from seeing a doctor? Here's where the answer's hiding. This is his assessment after the intake call on 02/09/2026. Clinical: the Run Report's neck stiffness, transport declined, no treatment yet, and we still need his own dated description and a first doctor's evaluation. Social: he lives with Margaret at 2214 Maple Hollow Rd, he owns no car, her Civic was damaged, and he carpools with Kevin Alvarez. So, {name}, there's your answer. How does a man with no car and a damaged family car get to a clinic? We don't know yet, and that question goes on the table. Pre-morbid: nothing on file, and it's written as an open question, not a blank. Vocational: shift lead at Northgate since 01/12/2026, 8-hour shifts at $22.00 an hour. The last row is a draft SMART goal, full 8-hour shifts by a dated review, waiting for the doctor to confirm the measure.
model.ask: {name}, which open question on this table would you close first, and why?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the desk. When the intake call is done, you record the four-area assessment in Case Notes, every area dated, and anything you don't know yet is listed as an open question. If an old injury comes up, you request those records through Medical Records Requests, and yes, the records office will play you the same hold song until you know every word, so request early, and write the before-the-crash picture as plain facts: body part, dates, doctor, outcome. Then you open the Action Plan Editor and write the SMART goals and the four care groups into the Clinical and Functional pillars, each with a measure, a date and an owner, and you ask the first doctor to confirm them. And when you spot a life problem, like no ride to care, you calendar it as a treatment risk and flag it before it becomes a gap. True story: a client I worked with missed three weeks of therapy because his ride was his cousin, and the cousin got a girlfriend. Three weeks. Nobody asked. That gap cost him on the offer. {name}, don't let a cousin's love life cost John Doe money.
job.ask: {name}, what would you set up this week so John Doe's ride never becomes a gap?

dodont.say: Let's close with 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides one Do or Don't about the assessment, the goals and the care plan. I'll show three clues, one at a time. Call Do or Don't and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it. {name}, your side's going first. Keep one line in mind while you play. Writing down exactly what a client tells you about an old injury is your job. Deciding whether that injury is related to the crash, or made worse by it, belongs to the doctor and to Atty. Thorne. Now here's your mystery for the road. The table says pre-morbid status is still an open question. {name}, before the next block, look through what's on John Doe's file and tell me one question you'd ask him on the next call to close it, worded so you're gathering facts and not giving an opinion.
dodont.ask: {name}, what's the one question you'd ask John Doe to learn how he was before the crash?

why.say: Quick show of hands. Who here has ever used a map app and ignored the route because you thought you knew a shortcut? Keep them up if it actually worked. Yeah, that's about what I thought. {name}, I saw your hand go down fast. Treatment works the same way. Every adjuster, every IME doctor, which is a doctor the insurance company hires to examine our client, and every defense lawyer will hold John Doe's records up against a standard map of how recovery is supposed to go. When care drifts off that map, that drift is the number one reason insurers deny treatment and order an IME. So you've got a choice. You can sit back, watch the recovery, and find out about the drift when the denial letter shows up. Or you can know the map, spot the drift first, ask the doctor why, and have the answer on file before anyone turns it into an argument. And there's one week on this map that adjusters circle in red. I'll tell you which one shortly.
why.ask: {name}, when a client's care drifts off schedule, who usually notices first: us, the adjuster, or defense counsel?

theory.say: Four ideas, in plain words. The Standard Treatment Map is the usual route of care after a crash, stop by stop: the ambulance and the emergency room, then imaging like X-rays and MRIs, then chiropractic care and therapy, then orthopedics, which are bone and joint specialists, and pain management, and only when it's serious, surgery and the care after it. If a stop gets skipped or taken out of order, there needs to be a medical reason on file. The Clinical Pathway asks one question at every check-in: is he getting better? Yes, care continues. No, and we're in what's called the variance loop, and what happens next is the doctor's decision. Variance analysis just means figuring out why he's off track before the insurer stops paying. And Reasonable and Necessary is the insurer's test for paying a bill: is this normal care for this kind of injury, and is he actually doing more, not just saying he hurts less? {name}, keep that last part in your pocket.
theory.ask: {name}, why would an insurer care more about a range-of-motion number than the client saying he feels better?

theory2.say: Here's the reveal I promised you. The week adjusters circle in red is week 6. That's the 6-Week Rule: by week 6 of care, the map expects 20 to 30 percent more range of motion or a lower pain score. If a client is still at ten out of ten after 12 therapy sessions, you raise it with the doctor now, not later. Next, the Red Flag Rule: no change in the disability score after 12 weeks of therapy is called a plateau, meaning progress has stalled, and the usual answer is a specialist or a second opinion. That's the doctor's call. Then objective metrics, which put recovery into numbers: the Oswestry or DASH questionnaires every 30 days, a walking test for leg injuries, the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 mood screens when progress stalls, and an FCE, a physical abilities test, before going back to work. Last, the Stakeholder Triad: the clinic, the lawyer and the insurer, with you passing information between them. {name}, quick check.
theory2.ask: {name}, who picks which of those measures a client gets, and who asks for them?

frame.say: Here's the map itself, phase by phase. Acute is days 1 to 14: the ER or urgent care, imaging, a brace, rest and ice, maybe first therapy, and our focus is proving the crash caused the injury and lining up PIP, the client's own insurance that pays Medical Bills no matter who's at fault. Sub-acute is weeks 2 to 8: active therapy two or three times a week and specialist visits, and we watch for real gains like range of motion. Restorative is weeks 9 to 24: work hardening, which is therapy that rebuilds job strength, injections, emotional support, and we look for anything blocking a return to work. Maintenance is six months on: home exercises and visits as needed, and the big question becomes MMI, Maximum Medical Improvement, meaning he's as good as he's going to get. Then discharge, maybe an impairment rating, which is the doctor's number for any lasting loss, and the file moves to paying off the Medical Bills. Every treatment here is somebody's order, and never ours. {name}, you're up.
frame.ask: {name}, John Doe's date of loss is 02/06/2026 and he hasn't been treated. Which phase was he in at intake, and what was our focus?

rules.say: Here's how you work the map, lazy version versus excellent version. The lazy Case Manager checks in, writes "client still treating," and hangs up. The excellent one counts the phase from the date of loss, counts the weeks of care from the first visit, puts him on the map every single check-in, and asks: is he improving? If not, you name the type of problem before anyone acts on it. Clinical, meaning a medical issue. Psychosocial, meaning life or mood is getting in the way. Or systemic, meaning the system's stuck, like an insurance approval that never came, or a clinic that is booked solid until next spring, and that's never the client's fault. You get the doctor's measurements on file. You raise concerns at week 6 and the 12-week plateau, not after a denial. A real red flag goes into A-C-T, Assess, Coordinate, Track, which you'll learn later today. Why bother? Because a demand that explains every bump in treatment gets paid. One with unexplained bumps gets cut. And through all of it, the doctor decides care and Atty. Thorne decides what it means for the case.
rules.ask: {name}, what's the difference between asking a doctor about a specialist and telling John Doe he needs one?

model.say: Let's put John Doe on the map as he stood at intake. Before I do, {name}, guess how many medical records we have. The answer is one. The EMS Run Report from 02/06/2026: neck stiffness, and he declined transport. So the map's emergency room stop never happened, and at intake he was in the acute phase with no care at all. On a typical file, this is when a first evaluation happens, right after an hour in the waiting room reading a magazine from three years ago, then imaging or early therapy if a doctor orders it. For us, every day without an evaluation is a fact on the timeline, Atty. Thorne hears about any gap, and our focus is getting causation facts on file and Harbor Point's $5,000 PIP confirmed in writing. Further along the table you can see what we'll watch later: attendance and week-6 measurements, anything blocking his return to work, and finally the doctor's MMI note. I had a client once who skipped the ER, skipped the doctor, and went straight to a massage place for a month. The adjuster called it a spa vacation. Don't let John's file get that nickname.
model.ask: {name}, if John Doe asks you whether he should go see a doctor, what can you say and what can't you say?

job.say: On the job, it looks like this. At every check-in with John Doe or a doctor's office, you open the treatment timeline in the CMS, write down his phase, his week from the date of loss and his week of care, and note whether he's improving, with the date. If he isn't, or a stop gets skipped, you label the type of problem and call the doctor's office to ask what's planned, and that answer goes in Case Notes. At week 6 of care and every 30 days after, you request the measurements. And when a problem could cost the claim, you send a Risk Flag to Atty. Thorne the same day, in the map's language, facts only. Here's the payoff. Months from now, when the adjuster asks why therapy paused in week 4, the answer is already in the file, dated, from the doctor. That's the difference between defending a number and watching it get cut. {name}, let's see how sharp your instincts are.
job.ask: {name}, what would make you flag a problem to Atty. Thorne the same day rather than at the next status report?

dodont.say: Let's close with 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides one Do or Don't about working the treatment map. I'll show three clues, one at a time. Call Do or Don't and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it. {name}, you're keeping score. While you play, keep one picture in mind. The map is a measuring stick, not a rulebook. A client who's off the map isn't wrong. He's unexplained until the doctor explains him. Your job is to get that explanation on file early, in plain words, and never to supply it yourself. Now your mystery. John Doe is in the acute phase, and day 14 of that phase is coming up fast. {name}, count it out from the date of loss and tell me the exact date the acute window closes, and what has to be on the file by then.
dodont.ask: {name}, counting from 02/06/2026, what date does John Doe's acute window close, and what must be on file by then?

why.say: Game time. Would you rather: have a client who calls you every single day, or a client who never calls at all? Left side of the room, every day. Right side, never. Go. {name}, defend your side in one sentence. Here's the twist. The client who never calls is the scary one, because silence is where cases quietly fall apart. At intake John Doe hadn't started treatment. All we know medically is the EMS report from 02/06/2026: neck stiffness, and he declined transport. But once care begins, you're the one person on this file who reads every record as it comes in and hears from him between visits. A red flag missed in a record, a yellow flag missed on a call, or a stall nobody talks about can quietly pull him off the plan his doctors set, and leave Atty. Thorne without the facts he needs. So here are two tools: a watch-list and a way of talking. And there's one specialty on that watch-list that adjusters pick apart harder than any other. Hold your guess.
why.ask: {name}, between appointments, who else on this file is actually hearing from John Doe?

map.say: Here's the road for this lesson, five stops. First, you read the records for red flags, meaning warning signs, by specialty: physical therapy, surgery, medication and mental health. Second, you listen on your calls for yellow flags, which are life and mood problems that get in the way of recovery, and you write them down in his own words. Third, you talk using OARS, which stands for open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries. Don't worry, I'll show you what each one sounds like. Fourth, you handle the mid-treatment plateau, the point where he stops improving and starts losing interest, by bringing him back to his own goal and asking whether the plan still fits. And last, you send it to the right person: medical danger goes to the doctor, legal danger goes to Atty. Thorne, and then A-C-T, that's Assess, Coordinate and Track, which we'll run properly later today. {name}, before we start, which stop on this road do you think will be the hardest for you?
map.ask: {name}, which of these five stops do you think a busy Case Manager skips first?

theory.say: You can't spot something off-track if you don't know what on-track looks like, so a Case Manager has to know the standard treatment patterns. A red flag is a step away from that pattern, and it signals one of three things: medical danger, a case that's stuck, or treatment being stretched out just to bill more. Physical therapy is the starting point of most care, so its flags tell you the case is stalling or being over-treated. Surgery is the most valuable part of a claim, so its flags are about safety and whether the care met the normal standard. And now the reveal: the specialty adjusters pick apart hardest is pain management and medication, because of opioid rules and audits on whether the drugs were truly needed. Medical danger, like a fever after surgery, goes to the doctor the same day. Legal danger goes to Atty. Thorne. {name}, did you guess medication? Be honest.
theory.ask: {name}, why do you think adjusters look hardest at medication, of all the specialties?

theory2.say: Four more ideas. Mental health and head-injury cases can be worth a lot, and they're handled carefully: the problem has to be tied to the crash and confirmed by a doctor. Yellow flags are life and mood barriers that knock recovery off course. Things like fear-avoidance, which is being afraid to move because it might hurt, catastrophizing, which is expecting the worst every time, usually right after a midnight appointment with Dr. Google, stress about the lawsuit, and leaning on pills or passive care like massage instead of doing the exercises. You'll hear these on the phone way more than you'll read them in a record. Motivational interviewing is a way of talking that keeps a client going once the newness wears off, by drawing out his own reasons to keep at it. And the mid-treatment plateau is when the excitement fades, the hard work starts, and attendance drops unless someone pulls him back in. {name}, you're going to be that someone.
theory2.ask: {name}, which of those yellow flags would you be most likely to miss on a quick call?

frame.say: Here are the red flags laid out by specialty. Before I read them, {name}, I'll make you sort each one into medical danger or legal danger as we go. In physical therapy, it's more than 12 sessions with no gain in movement or pain and no referral, which means the case is stuck. Or it's only heat, TENS, a little electrical stimulation device, or massage, with no real exercise, which adjusters write off. In surgery, it's surgery recommended before therapy or injections when it's not an emergency, which makes the insurer question whether it was needed. Or a fever, redness or sharp pain after surgery that someone says can wait until the follow-up. That one's medical danger, and the doctor hears about it today. In medication, it's an opioid, a muscle relaxant and a sedative together, doses going up, or a drug test that doesn't match the prescriptions. And in mental health, it's vague life-stress notes, or head-injury symptoms first reported months later.
frame.ask: {name}, which row on this table would you treat as medical danger rather than legal danger?

rules.say: Here's the line between lazy and excellent. The lazy Case Manager files the therapy notes without reading them. The excellent one reads every note against the watch-list. You spot a red flag and report it, and the doctor judges it. In therapy, watch for no gain after 12 sessions, passive-only care, and two or more missed visits. In surgery, watch for surgery before simpler care was tried, a left and right mix-up, and anything after surgery that someone wants to leave until the follow-up. In medication, watch for what's called the Holy Trinity, that opioid, relaxant and sedative combo, plus rising doses and drug test mismatches. Raise them with the prescriber as facts and a question, never an accusation. In mental health and head injuries, write down the date every symptom was first reported, because a symptom that shows up late looks made up to the defense. Record yellow flags in his words. And at the plateau, bring him back to his goal. If he's not reaching it, it's usually the plan, not the person.
rules.ask: {name}, if a client says his pain pills make him drowsy at work, what do you say to him, and who do you call?

model.say: Here's what OARS sounds like on John Doe's calls once care begins. These lines are examples, written for his first weeks of care. An open question, one he can't answer with yes or no: walk me through how your neck has been since the collision. An affirmation, which recognizes his effort: nice work getting that first appointment booked. A reflection, which repeats back what you heard: it sounds like the stiffness makes a full shift feel a long way off. A summary pulls the call together and asks what you missed. Then two moves. Say he's told you full shifts at Northgate are his goal, and therapy starts to feel pointless. You set those two things side by side and let him answer. And if he pushes back on a clinic, you don't argue. You ask why, and take his reason to the doctor. I once heard a Case Manager ask a client, "You're doing your exercises, right?" The client said yes. He'd been using the resistance band to hold up his tomato plants. {name}, open questions catch that. Yes-or-no questions don't.
model.ask: {name}, what does the file lose if your note says “catastrophizing” instead of his own sentence?

job.say: Here's how it looks on the desk. Every time a treatment record, prescription record or bill comes in, usually by fax, forty pages at a time, in an order only the fax machine understands, you read it against the red-flag list and log any flag in Risk Flags, with the record it came from and the date you first saw it. If it's medical danger, like a fever after surgery or a medication concern, you call the doctor's office that same day, note the call in Case Notes, run A-C-T and tell Atty. Thorne. And once John Doe's care starts, every check-in runs on OARS, with specific questions about visits, pain and what he can actually do. Any yellow flag goes in his own words, and the GIRP note, which is just a structured call note covering goal, intervention, response and plan, gets written the same day. Why does the date you first saw it matter? Because months later, someone will ask when the firm knew. A dated log protects the client, the firm, and the settlement. {name}, here's the question that ties it together.
job.ask: {name}, why log the date you first saw a flag, and not only the date on the record?

dodont.say: Let's close with 3 Clues, 1 Rule. Each round hides one Do or Don't about red flags, yellow flags and how we talk to clients. I'll show three clues, one at a time. Call Do or Don't as soon as you've got it, and name the rule. Every right call counts, on whichever clue you make it. {name}, your team's up first. While you play, keep one line in mind. You can listen, reflect, and keep John Doe engaged in the plan his doctors set. You can't tell him that missing visits will hurt his case, and you can't decide a test, a medication or a referral. Now here's your mystery to take into the activity. We already know John has no car, lives with his mother, and just started a new job at Northgate. {name}, before his first appointment is even booked, which yellow flag is most likely to show up on our next call, and what open question would you use to find out?
dodont.ask: {name}, which yellow flag do you predict for John Doe, and what open question would uncover it?

why.say: Quick game. True or false: car insurance works the same in every state. {name}, you're first. If you said true, welcome to the club of every new Case Manager ever. It's false. PIP, which is the client's own insurance that pays Medical Bills no matter who caused the crash, is written state by state. And Florida has a rule that can decide, within days of the accident, whether PIP pays any medical at all, and whether the client has $2,500 or $10,000 to draw on. It's called the Emergency Medical Condition rule, EMC for short. Miss it and no demand letter fixes it later. Florida, the only state where the insurance rules have as many twists as the weather. Now, John Doe's file is in Riverton. Riverton is an add-on PIP state with no EMC rule, so his $5,000 of Harbor Point PIP isn't capped by one. But the day you open a Florida file, the clock starts at the date of loss, and you're the one who calendars it. There's one person on John's own file who could never make the EMC call. I'll tell you who in a minute.
why.ask: {name}, before you apply any PIP rule to a file, what's the first fact you need to check?

rules.say: Here's Florida's rule, Fla. Stat. section 627.736. PIP is $10,000, paying 80% of reasonable medical expenses and 60% of lost income. Initial care has to happen within 14 days after the accident, or PIP pays nothing for medical. The full $10,000 is there only if an MD, a DO, a dentist, a physician assistant or an advanced practice registered nurse determines there was an Emergency Medical Condition, meaning an injury serious enough that going without care could seriously harm the client. Without that finding, medical stops at $2,500. A chiropractor can give the initial care but can't make the EMC finding, and massage and acupuncture aren't covered. So there's the reveal: John's chiropractor couldn't make that call. Had John's file been in Florida, 02/20/2026 was day 14, the last day inside the window. The lazy Case Manager thinks "he'll get around to a doctor." The excellent one has day 14 on the calendar before the client's even home from the tow yard. And always confirm the current statute, because legislatures love a sequel.
rules.ask: {name}, a Florida client is first seen on day 14 by a physician assistant. Is he inside the window, and can that provider make the EMC finding?

job.say: Let's walk a Florida file. At intake you calendar the 14-day initial-care deadline from the date of loss, and you tell the client that deadline and where and when care is available. That's facts and logistics, never a medical recommendation. When the first record arrives, you check three things: the date against day 14, who saw him, and whether an EMC determination is written down. If a qualifying provider's record doesn't have one, you ask the office whether it was assessed and request it in the records. You keep the $2,500 or $10,000 bucket current in the PIP Log, our running record of every PIP payment, and a missing EMC or a late first visit goes to Atty. Thorne the same day. The provider decides the EMC; Atty. Thorne decides what it means. I once watched a Florida client lose every dollar of PIP medical because his first visit landed on day 15. The client said he was waiting for the swelling to go down. The swelling went down. So did his coverage. Here's your mystery for the next block: what could you have told that client on day one, without giving medical advice, that would have changed everything? {name}, I want your exact words.
job.ask: {name}, a Florida client's first visit is with a chiropractor on day 10. What's covered, and what's still missing?
